title: In-situ growth of CuO/Cu nanocomposite electrode for efficient CO2 electroreduction to CO with bacterial cellulose as support
abstract: Bacterial cellulose (BC) with large surface area and hydrophilic surface property is considered to be a good potential porous substrate for the deposition of active materials for catalysis, but lacks electrical conductivity for desired electrocatalysis application. By applying an in-situ chemical reduction, we here report a self-standing, BC-supported catalyst electrode of highly dispersed Cu and CuO nanocomposites (CuO/Cu4:3@BC) for catalyzing efficient CO2 electroreduction to CO. The inherent three-dimensional web-like porous structure of the BC substrate is sustained without further carbonization of the electrode. Compared to the conventional carbon papersupported CuO/Cu composite catalysts, the as-prepared CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode demonstrates an outstanding charge transport property and higher current density for CO2 reduction, owing to superiority of the web-like porous structure of the BC substrate with more accessible active sites to electrolytes and faster transfer of reactants and products. Therefore, the architecturally arranged CuO/Cu composite catalysts of the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode offer unique structural advantages of good ion and charge transport, promoting the catalytic kinetics for the conversion of CO2 to CO. The resulting electrode affords CO with a faradaic efficiency of 53 % at a small overpotential of 490mV, and a durable activity over 40 h.

In-situ growth of CuO/Cu nanocomposite electrode for efficient CO2 electroreduction to CO with bacterial cellulose as support
Yue Zhoua, Xiaojing Guoa, Xuanjiang Lic, Jing Fud,**, Junyu Liua, Feng Hongc, Jinli Qiaoa,b,* a State Key Laboratory for Modification of Chemical Fibers and Polymer Materials, College of Environmental Science and Engineering, Donghua University, 2999 Ren’min North Road, Shanghai 201620, China b Shanghai Institute of Pollution Control and Ecological Security, Shanghai 200092, China c College of Chemistry, Chemical Engineering & Biotechnology, Donghua University, 2999 Ren’min North Road, Shanghai 201620, China d School of Materials Science and Engineering, Tongji University, Shanghai 201804, China
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: Bacterial cellulose In-situ chemical reduction CO2 electroreduction Copper/copper oxide Carbon monoxide
A B S T R A C T
Bacterial cellulose (BC) with large surface area and hydrophilic surface property is considered to be a good potential porous substrate for the deposition of active materials for catalysis, but lacks electrical conductivity for desired electrocatalysis application. By applying an in-situ chemical reduction, we here report a self-standing, BC-supported catalyst electrode of highly dispersed Cu and CuO nanocomposites (CuO/Cu4:3@BC) for catalyzing efficient CO2 electroreduction to CO. The inherent three-dimensional web-like porous structure of the BC substrate is sustained without further carbonization of the electrode. Compared to the conventional carbon papersupported CuO/Cu composite catalysts, the as-prepared CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode demonstrates an outstanding charge transport property and higher current density for CO2 reduction, owing to superiority of the web-like porous structure of the BC substrate with more accessible active sites to electrolytes and faster transfer of reactants and products. Therefore, the architecturally arranged CuO/Cu composite catalysts of the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode offer unique structural advantages of good ion and charge transport, promoting the catalytic kinetics for the conversion of CO2 to CO. The resulting electrode affords CO with a faradaic efficiency of 53 % at a small overpotential of 490mV, and a durable activity over 40 h.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Electrochemical CO2 reduction (ECR-CO2) is attracting extensive attention for direct production of fuels and value added industrial chemicals, such as C1 products (HCOOH and CO) and C2 products (C2H5OH, C2H4) [1–4], as these reactions would be economically practical through combining the renewable wind and solar power system [5–7]. As the essential and typical C1 products, HCOOH is widely used in various industries due to its high energy density, such as being the fuel for fuel cells, the neutralizer in leather, and the raw materials for the formation of pesticides [7,8]. In addition to HCOOH, CO is a critical part of syngas, which can yield synthetic petroleum and hydrocarbon fuels using Fischer–Tropsch methods [4,9,10]. Compared to other organic chemicals, it is relatively easier for the electroreduction CO2 to CO due to the two-electron reduction process [11,12], according to the following possible reduction reactions (pH=7, 25 °C, 1 atm) [13].
CO2 + 2H+ + 2e― = CO + H2O E(SHE)0 = – 0.52 V (1)
2H+ + 2e―= H2 E(SHE)0= – 0.42 V (2)
The form of CO2•− plays an essential role in the reaction of ECR-CO2 which is the rate-determining step (RDS) and determines the distribution of the final product [14]. However, the process of Eq. (1) suffers from a high overpotential, because the CO2 is an extremely stable liner molecule, and is often competing with the undesired hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) [15]. As a result, it is urgently needed to develop efficient catalysts with high selectivity and activity for the generation of CO and other products (such as HCOOH, CH4 and C2H4, etc).
Various types of catalysts such as metals [16,17], metallic oxide [18,19], and carbon-based materials [20,21] have been explored for ECR-CO2 in aqueous alkaline solutions. Noble metal catalysts, such as Au and Ag [4,22–26], have achieved excellent Faradaic efficiency (FE) of CO formation that can exceed 80 %. Nevertheless, their large-scale

application is seriously limited by their high cost and low earth abundance. Therefore, non-noble metal-based alternatives are getting more attentions to reduce the system cost [27]. Cu [28,29], Zn and In exhibited high selectivity for CO production [30–32], in particular, Cubased catalysts have demonstrated high capability in producing not only the CO, but also the hydrocarbons of formic acid, CH4, C2H4 and C2H5OH [6,19,33]. Unfortunately, much higher overpotentials (e.g., 490−690mV) were often required compared to those of the noble metal catalysts [27,34]. To this end, nanostructured Cu and Cu-based catalysts have been developed to increase the number of active sites for promoting the product selectivity and activity [29].
Despite of the catalysts development, their dispersion and assembly to the electrode are often limited by the lack of suitable support/substrate. Electrically conductive carbon-based gas diffusion electrodes (GDE) are commonly used as the support for this application, albeit with their limitations such as: (i) addition of non-conductive polymeric binders, (ii) limited planar surface area for low loading of catalysts, (iii) time-consuming and complicated electrode coating procedure and (iv) agglomerated and non-uniform structure of the catalyst assembly [3,35]. Given the aforementioned limitations of using GDE as the catalyst support/substrate, environmental-friendly bacterial cellulose (BC) consisting of a web-like, ultra-fine network of cellulose nanofibers (20–100 nm) is a good choice for the formation of self-supported, highsurface-area substrate for loading catalysts for CO2 reduction. BC membranes produced by microbial fermentation can provide extremely high specific surface area that is about 200 times larger than that of coniferous plant cellulose [36]. Moreover, their tremendous hydroxyl groups (eOH) can effectively anchor metal cations for surface engineering [37]. BC supported palladium with higher thermal stability and lower gas crossover has also been reported as the proton-exchange membrane for the membrane electrode assemblies application, in which the palladium nanoclusters were precipitated with the reducing groups of BC, and generated higher surface area with catalytic efficiency within the structure of BC [38]. For the electrode substrate application, BC-derived NiS/carbon aerogels were prepared with a gelation–carbonization process and reported as an alternative to carbon paper-supported electrode for supercapacitors [39], although the inherent structure of BC suffered from a certain degree of collapse under the high temperature carbonation.
Inspired by the above completion, in this study, we report a selfstanding, BC-supported catalyst electrode of dispersed Cu and CuO nanocomposites (CuO/Cu4:3@BC) for CO2 electroreduction to CO. The electrode is prepared by an in-situ chemical reduction method, by which the electrode activity can be tailored by the surface Cu0 and Cu2+ composition. Compared with the carbon paper-supported CuO/ Cu composite catalyst electrode, the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode possesses higher accessible active surface area and lower charge transfer resistance. Therefore, more efficient ECR-CO2 process is realized resulting from their web-like, open porous structure and 3D architecturally arranged CuO/Cu composite catalysts. This work demonstrates BC’s superiority as efficient electrode substrate on supporting electrocatalysts for CO2 reduction.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials
sections.text: Citric acid monohydrate (C6H8O7·H2O, purity ≥ 99.5 %), copper sulfate pentahydrate (CuSO4·5H2O, purity ≥ 99.0 %), D(+)-Glucose monohydrate (C6H12O6·H2O), sodium hydroxide (NaOH, purity ≥ 96.0 %) and sodium borohydride (NaBH4, 98 wt%) were all purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Shanghai Co. Ltd. Tryptone was received by China pharmaceutical (group) Shanghai chemical reagent Co. Ltd. Ethanol (C2H5OH, purity ≥ 99.7 %, AR) was provided by China Changshu Hong sheng Fine Chemical Co. Ltd. All the reagents used in the experiment were received without any purified.

sections.heading: 2.2. Synthesis of CuO/Cu@BC electrode
sections.text: The Cu and CuO nanoparticles supported on BC membranes were prepared by an in-situ chemical reduction method [40,41]. In this work, 0.4M CuSO4·5H2O was dissolved in 70 % mixed solution of ethanol and water (15mL deionized water, 35mL ethanol). The BC membranes with a geometric area of 2 cm×2 cm were soaked in the mixed solution and stirred for 24 h. Then NaBH4 (0.2M, 0.3M, 0.4M) as reducing agent and 0.1M NaOH were dissolved in 50mL deionized water and finally added to above solution in a warm bath at 30 °C for 90min. After that the BC membranes were washed with running deionized water to remove the superficial chemicals. These prepared samples were referred to as CuO/Cu4:2@BC, CuO/Cu4:3@BC, CuO/ Cu4:4@BC according to the different concentration of NaBH4 (0.2M, 0.3 M, 0.4M).

sections.heading: 2.3. Characterization of CuO/Cu@BC
sections.text:
The microscopic morphology of the prepared CuO/Cu@BC composite film was analyzed by field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM, S-4800, Hitachi, Japan). The obtained samples were freezedried under −40 °C, and a small amount of conductive paste was used to fix the sample stage before vacuum gold plating. The accelerating voltage range is 0.5–30 KV, and the magnification range is 20–100,000.
High-resolution transmission electron microscope (HR-TEM; JEM2100 F, Japan) were conducted for the crystal structures and morphology characterization, where the samples of CuO/Cu@BC were freeze-dried under −40 °C and ultrasonicated for 30min before being examined.
The crystal structure of CuO/Cu@BC was analyzed by X-ray diffractometer (XRD, D/Max-2550 PC, Japan Rigaku) with Cu-Ka1 radiation at 40 kV and 300mA.
The surface chemical compositions were evaluated by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, PHI-5400, U.S.A.).

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical measurements
sections.text:
The H-type electrochemical cell was used for electrochemical measurements on a CHI760E electrochemical workstation. The Nafion 117 membrane was utilized for separating the anode and cathode compartment. The experiments were conducted by a three-electrode system and the Pt sheet was used as counter electrode, facing the CuO/ Cu@BC electrode, a saturated silver chloride electrode (Ag/AgCl) served as the reference electrode. All potentials measured in this work were relative to RHE using: ERHE (V) = EAg/AgCl (V) + 0.197 V + (0.0591 V×pH). The 0.5M KHCO3 aqueous solution served as the electrolyte, which was bubbled with N2 (99.999 %) for at least 30min until the air in the cathode compartment being removed (pH=8.3) before the measurement of CO2 reduction. The CO2 (99.99 %) finally was also bubbled to the cathode compartment like N2 (pH=7.4) and continuously bubbled through the test to maintain the pH of the electrolyte.
The electrochemical active area tests of all electrode were measured by double-layer capacitance on CHI760E electrochemical workstation [34]. The test related with cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves was measured in N2-saturated 0.5M KHCO3 electrolyte and the CVs were measured at different scan rates with wide potential streets from 0.23 to -0.07 VRHE, where no conversion and reduction of CO2 occurred. Finally, a graph of the relationship between current density and different scan rates of CVs was plotted. The slope of the fitting straight line equaled to the capacitance of the electrode.
The electrochemical impedance tests of the prepared CuO/Cu@BC and CuO/Cu@GDE were estimated by Nyquist spectrogram with the frequency ranging from 100 kHz to 0.1 Hz at the initial potential of -0.5 VRHE.

sections.heading: 2.5. Electrolyte product analysis
sections.text: The reduction gas products of ECR-CO2 were measured by a gas chromatograph (GC1120, Shanghai Sunny Hengping Scientific Instrument Co. Ltd). The organic gases were tested by flame ionization detector (FID), while some inorganic gases like H2, CO were measured by thermal conductivity detector (TCD). The liquid products were quantified by ion chromatography (IC1820, Shanghai Sunny Hengping Scientific Instrument Co. Ltd). The specific calculation of all the products is demonstrated in the supporting information.

sections.heading: 3.1. Morphological and structural characterization of CuO/Cu4:3@BC
sections.text:
The CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode was prepared by a room-temperature in-situ chemical reduction method, as is schematically illustrated in Fig. 1a. Firstly, BC hydrogel was prepared by the traditional static mode (supporting information). The BC hydrogel with fibrous structure is then soaked in an ethanol-water mixture solution of copper sulfate for 24 h to have Cu2+ absorbing on its surface. Such absorption is realized by the electrostatic interaction between Cu cations and the hydroxyl groups of the BC [37]. After the initial Cu2+ nucleation period, the Cu2+@BC reacts with NaBH4 solution and in-situ reduces the absorbed Cu2+ to CuO and Cu nanocomposites on the BC surface. The morphology of the pristine BC hydrogel and the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode was examined by scanning electron microscopy (SEM). As shown in Fig. S1, the pristine BC hydrogel shows an interconnected web-like 3D porous network consisting of nanofibers with a diameter of 30−100 nm. The unique web-like structure allows multiple open channels and available surface areas favourable for the in-situ crystallization process of CuO/Cu nanocomposites formation. As shown in Fig. 1b, a clear colour change of the BC electrode from opaque to reddish black can be observed after the in-situ growth of CuO/Cu nanocomposites. The resulting CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode exhibits a high
degree of mechanical flexibility under bending condition. Fig. 1c provides the SEM image and corresponding element mapping of the CuO/ Cu4:3@BC electrode, in which Cu, O and C atoms are homogeneously distributed on the fibrous electrode surface. The crystal phases of CuO (111), CuO (002), CuO (220) (JCPDS: 48-1548) and Cu (111), Cu (220), Cu (200) (JCPDS: 04-0836) of the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode were detected by XRD analysis (Fig. 1d). The presence of Cu and CuO crystal phases can be observed more directly in the high-resolution TEM image of the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode (Fig. 1e), in which the inter planar spacings of 0.208 nm, 0.180 nm and 0.231 nm are assigned to the (111) and (200) plane of Cu and the (111) plane of CuO, respectively.
Fig. 2a–b illustrates the Cu2+ nucleation and crystallization processes occurring on the BC surfaces, which are further investigated by tailoring the molar ratio of NaBH4 and CuSO4 reaction solutions. As can be seen from Fig. 2a–b, when the molar ratio of the CuSO4 to NaBH4 is 4:2, the surface of the as-prepared electrode (referred to as the CuO/ Cu4:2@BC electrode) shows unevenly distributed flake-like deposits on the surface of the nanofibers. XRD analysis of the CuO/Cu4:2@BC electrodes (Fig. S2) reveals that the deposits consist of CuO (002), CuO (111), CuO (220) (JCPDS: 48-1548) and Cu type of (111) and (200) (JCPDS: 04-0836). As increasing the NaBH4 concentration (i.e, the molar ratio of CuSO4 to NaBH4 is 4:3), the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode surface indicates a uniform coverage with nanoparticles (50−70 nm) evenly decorated on the top BC fiber surfaces (Fig. 2c–d). With further increasing the NaBH4 concentration, where the molar ratio of CuSO4 to NaBH4 is 4:4, larger particles with sizes in approximately 100 nm are formed on the BC fiber surfaces (Fig. 2e–f), indicating a crystal aggregation during the crystallization process of the CuO/Cu4:4@BC electrode. XRD analysis of the CuO/Cu@BC electrodes in different CuSO4 to NaBH4 ratios further reveals that the deposits consist of crystal CuO (JCPDS: 48–1548) and Cu (JCPDS: 04-0836), which is identical to the SEM results (Fig. S2).
Fig. 3 shows the electrode surface chemical properties, which were examined by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). As displayed in Fig. 3, the high-resolution Cu2p spectra of all the three electrodes
exhibits two distinct peaks at 951.5 eV and 931.5 eV corresponding to Cu2p1/2 and Cu2p3/2, respectively. Characteristic peaks of deconvolution of Cu2p at 953.6 eV and 933.7 eV correspond to the binding energy of Cu2+ from the CuO, and the peaks of 951.5 eV and 931.5 eV are ascribed to the metallic Cu. As increasing the concentration of NaBH4 in the reaction solutions, the relative ratio of Cu0/Cu2+ firstly decreases from 3.60 (CuO/Cu4:2@BC electrode) to 1.44 (CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode), and then increases to 2.08 for the CuO/Cu4:4@BC electrode. Given the highest mass and specific activities of the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode as discussed below, it can be concluded that the Cu2+ sites tend to be more active than the metallic Cu, while the metallic Cu sites may play an important role in electron transport for the CO2 electrocatalysis.

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrocatalytic activity and performance of CuO/Cu@BC for
sections.text:
ECR−CO2
The electrochemical performance of the CuO/Cu4:2@BC, CuO/ Cu4:3@BC and CuO/Cu4:4@BC electrodes were evaluated in an H-type electrochemical cell in 0.5M KHCO3 (Fig. 4a). The CO2 electroreduction of three different electrodes was first analyzed by CV. As shown in Fig. S3, all the electrodes tested in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte exhibit a higher current density than that obtained in N2-saturated electrolyte at a more positive potential, indicating that the electrocatalytic activity of the electrodes originates from CuO/Cu sites. The current density between CO2- and N2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 of the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode shows the largest difference of 7mA cm−2 among all the electrodes, suggesting that the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode possesses a better catalytic activity. Moreover, linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves of all electrodes measured in CO2-saturated 0.5 M
KHCO3 with the rate of 5mV m s-1 were further conducted to investigate the catalytic activity of the electrodes. As shown in Fig. 4a, the current density of the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode reaches 21.77mA cm-2 at the potential of -0.81 VRHE, which is almost four times greater than that of the CuO/Cu4:2@BC electrode. The current density of all the electrodes at the most negative potential of -0.81 VRHE follows the order: CuO/Cu4:3@BC (21.77mA cm-2)> CuO/Cu4:4@BC (11.83mA cm-2)>CuO/Cu4:2@BC (6.67mA cm-2).
For a clear understanding of the origin of the enhanced activity of CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode for ECR-CO2, the specific activities of CuO/ Cu4:2@BC, CuO/Cu4:3@BC and CuO/Cu4:4@BC electrodes were evaluated by the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA). As shown in Fig. 4b and Fig. S4, the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode owns the largest double layer capacitances (12m F cm−2) than those of the CuO/Cu4:4@ BC (3m F cm-2) and CuO/Cu4:2@BC (2.8m F cm-2) electrodes. The results indicate that the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode possesses the largest electrochemical active area due to the direct ratio relation between double layer capacitance and electrochemical surface area. The BETnominalized catalytic activity analyzed by the LSV curves of various electrodes normalized by physical specific surface area (Fig. 4c) manifests a similar performance improvement trend to the previeous result in Fig. 4a, where the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode exihibits the highest catalytic activity than the other two electrodes. Learning from the previous SEM images (Fig. 2c–d), the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode with evenly distribution of CuO/Cu depositions endows the largest active surface area for catalysing CO2 electroreduction. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was further performed to evaluate the ion and electron transport behavior of the electrodes during the electrocatalysis (Fig. 4d). Intriguingly, the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode displays the smallest charge-transfer resistance among the three electrodes,
indicative of the highest electrochemical kinetics of the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode with optimal CuO/Cu composition and larger electrochemically active surface area.
To evaluate the electrochemical performance of the BC as the electrode substrate, a carbon paper-supported CuO/Cu4:3 catalyst electrode (CuO/Cu4:3@GDE) prepared by the conventional spray coating method was examined for a good comparison. Fig. 5a shows the LSV curves of the two electrodes, which were measured in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 with the rate of 5mV m s−1. The CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode exhibits an onset potential of -0.21 VRHE, more 40mV positive than that of CuO/Cu4:3@GDE electrode. Moreover, the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode produces a higher current density than that of the CuO/ Cu4:3@GDE electrode, indicating better catalytic activity for CO2 reduction. As shown in Fig. 5b and Fig. S4(b, d), the double layer capacitance of the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode is about 3-folds of the CuO/ Cu4:3@GDE electrode, implying that the 3D open porous structure of BC as the substrate favors for larger electrochemical active surface area. In
addition, the specific surface area of CuO/Cu4:3@BC is apparently larger than that of CuO/Cu4:3@GDE electrode according to Table S1, which demonstrates that the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode favors for the absorption of CO2 in the electrolytes. Further from the EIS results (Fig. 5c), it can be seen that the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode possesses a much lower charge transfer resistance superior to CuO/Cu4:3@GDE electrode, albeit a slightly higher contact resistance than those of the CuO/Cu4:3@GDE electrode. Evidently, the 3D web-like porous structure of the BC facilitates both ion and charge transport. A close observation of the CuO/Cu4:3@GDE electrode surface indicates that the CuO/Cu catalysts deposited on the carbon paper appear large particle aggregation and unevenly distribution (Fig. S5), leading to the reduction of the effective exposure of active sites and ion channels for CO2 electroreduction.

sections.heading: 3.3. Product analysis of CuO/Cu@BC for ECR-CO2
sections.text:
The ECR-CO2 performance of the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode was further assessed by chronoamperometry in constant potential electrolysis [8]. The current densities of the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode were measured in different electrolysis potentials. Fig. 6a shows that there is a positive correlation between the electrolysis current density and potentials, wherein the current density intensifies from 0.5 to 9mA cm−2
as potentials increase. Fig. 6b shows the chronoamperometry for CuO/ Cu4:3@BC electrode at different potentials for 1 h continuous electrolysis. The highest current density can be found at −0.7 VRHE, which matches well with the current density trend in Fig. 6a. To examine the selectivity of the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode, the Faradaic efficiencies (FE) for the reduction products at different potentials are illustrated in Fig. 6c. CO and H2 account for the major two reduction products at all tested potentials, while a minor portion of HCOOH products is detected by ion chromatography. The FE of HCOOH reaches a maximum of 7.83 % at the potential of -0.5 VRHE. The CO was detected after electrolysis at -0.4 VRHE, equivalent to an overpotential of 290mV. The FE of CO formation reaches a maximum of 53 % at the potential of -0.6 VRHE, which exceeds that of the polycrystalline Cu and annealed Cu [34]. The H2 is also suppressed to the utmost extent and the FE decreased to 44 % at the potential of -0.6 VRHE. Besides, the FE of electrodes prepared in different mole ratio between CuSO4 and NaBH4 were shown in Fig. S6, and it should be mentioned that the lowest ratio of Cu0/Cu2+ (CuO/ Cu4:3@BC) shows the best performance of ECR−CO2. The results highlight that the evenly distributed CuO/Cu nanocomposites on the web-like, porous BC substrate ensure large accessible active sites to electrolytes for efficient CO2 electroreduction to CO. As illustrated in Fig. S7, the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode obviously shows much higher FE of CO when compared to CuO/Cu4:3@GDE electrode. The FE for CO formation of CuO/Cu4:3@GDE reaches only 24 % at the potential of -0.6 VRHE and generates much more H2. Comparatively, the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode performs well in the reduction of CO2 to CO at a relatively low
potential (Table S2). In addition to the high activity, the stability test of CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode was analyzed by controlled potential electrolysis (CPE) [42]. As shown in Fig. 6d, even after 40 h electrolysis under a constant potential of -0.6 VRHE, the current density of CuO/ Cu4:3@BC electrode shows neglectable changes, indicative of a high stability of the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode was prepared by an insitu chemical reduction method. The CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode, with optimal CuO/Cu composition and high active surface area, stands out as the efficient electrode with high activity for CO2 electroreduction to CO. As a result, the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode exhibited a high FE of 53 % for CO formation at a low overpotential of 490mV. Detailed electrochemical performance evaluation including the mass and specific activates of the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode was applied to confirm the enhanced electrocatalytic performance, which stems from the higher ratio of CuO and larger electrochemically active surface area on the electrode. Meanwhile, the CuO/Cu4:3@BC electrode demonstrated a high stability in over 40 h continuous electrolysis without activity degradation. As the self-supported electrode, it utilizes the environmentalfriendly and high-surface-area BC as the catalyst substrate, which is of great advantage in facilitating charge and mass transport compared to the conventional carbon paper-supported powdery catalyst electrodes. Hence, the strategy of using BC as the substrate could be a guideline for designing high-performance electrode to improve performance of ECRCO2 with high efficiency and scalability.
